title: Question (which hereditary classes are poly-χ-bounded?)
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. Many classes are known to be $\chi$-bounded, but the proofs frequently give fast-growing binding functions, and it is natural to ask whether this is necessary. Esperet conjectured that every $\chi$-bounded hereditary class is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, but this was recently disproved by Briański, Davies and Walczak, leaving the question of which hereditary classes are. As a contribution, the authors prove that for every $k$ the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole (an induced subgraph with $k$ components, each a cycle of length at least four) is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, and similar results when the cycles are required to be odd or of length four, or long or of length four.
notes: Posed as a guiding open question in the introduction after noting Esperet's conjecture was disproved; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

title: Open problem (poly-χ-bounded for k-multihole with only odd cycles)
statement_text: For any integer $k \geq 1$, is the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which all the cycles have odd length polynomially $\chi$-bounded?
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A hole is an induced cycle of length at least four, and a $k$-multihole of $G$ is an induced subgraph with exactly $k$ components, each a cycle of length at least four (so graphs with no $1$-multihole are chordal, hence perfect). Scott and Seymour showed that the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which all the cycles have odd length is $\chi$-bounded, but it contains the class of $\{P_5,C_5\}$-free graphs, which the authors cannot yet prove to be polynomially $\chi$-bounded. The same applies to excluding $k$-multiholes whose cycles all have length at least $\ell$. The authors prove polynomial $\chi$-boundedness once cycles of length four are also permitted as components: for each $k$, the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which every component has length four or odd length is polynomially $\chi$-bounded (and similarly with length four or at least $\ell$).
notes: Stated as an open limitation in the introduction; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

title: Open problem (poly-χ-bounded for k-multihole with only long cycles)
statement_text: For any integers $k \geq 1$ and $\ell \geq 0$, is the class of graphs with no $k$-multihole in which all the cycles have length at least $\ell$ polynomially $\chi$-bounded?
context_text: This class is $\chi$-bounded for every $\ell \geq 0$ by [10], but the authors state they cannot yet prove it is poly-$\chi$-bounded, for the same reason as the odd-cycle case.
notes: Stated as an open limitation in the introduction; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

title: Informal conjecture (polynomial Gyárfás–Sumner)
statement_text: It might be true that every forest $H$ is good, i.e., the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded (strengthening the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture from $\chi$-boundedness to polynomial $\chi$-boundedness).
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A forest $H$ is good if the class of $H$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded. The Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture says that for every forest $H$ the class of $H$-free graphs is $\chi$-bounded; the statement here is the strengthening to polynomial binding functions. It has been proved only for a few simple kinds of trees and some (not all) forests that are disjoint unions of these; for instance, trees of diameter three are good, and stars and four-vertex paths are good. It is not even known that the disjoint union of two good trees is good. The authors introduce self-isolation as a tool: if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are good forests and one of them is self-isolating, then their disjoint union is good, where a graph $H$ is self-isolating if for every non-decreasing polynomial $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a polynomial $\phi$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$ has a set $A\subseteq V(G)$ with $\chi(G[A])>\psi(\omega(G[A]))$ such that either $G[A]$ is $H$-free, or $G$ contains an induced copy of $H$ whose vertex set is disjoint from $A$ and has no edges to $A$.
notes: Introduced with 'It might be true that'; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes

title: Open problem (disjoint union of good trees)
statement_text: It is not known that if trees $H_1$, $H_2$ are good (i.e., the class of $H_i$-free graphs is polynomially $\chi$-bounded for $i=1,2$), then the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is also good.
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. It might be true that every forest is good (a polynomial strengthening of the Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture), but this is only proved for a few simple trees. For instance trees of diameter three are good, but as far as the authors know disjoint unions of them might not be. A graph $H$ is self-isolating if for every non-decreasing polynomial $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a polynomial $\phi$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$ has a set $A\subseteq V(G)$ with $\chi(G[A])>\psi(\omega(G[A]))$ such that either $G[A]$ is $H$-free, or $G$ contains an induced copy of $H$ whose vertex set is disjoint from $A$ and has no edges to $A$. The authors show that if $H_1$ and $H_2$ are good forests and one of them is self-isolating, then their disjoint union is good; stars and four-vertex paths are good and self-isolating, so disjoint unions with them preserve goodness.

title: Question (are all graphs self-isolating?)
statement_text: Could it be that all graphs are self-isolating?
context_text: A class of graphs is hereditary if it is closed under taking induced subgraphs; a hereditary class is $\chi$-bounded if there is a function $\phi$ (a binding function) with $\chi(G)\le\phi(\omega(G))$ for every $G$ in the class, and polynomially $\chi$-bounded (poly-$\chi$-bounded) if $\phi$ can be taken to be a polynomial. A graph is $H$-free if it has no induced subgraph isomorphic to $H$. A graph $H$ is self-isolating if for every non-decreasing polynomial $\psi:\mathbb{N}\to\mathbb{N}$ there is a polynomial $\phi$ such that every graph $G$ with $\chi(G)>\phi(\omega(G))$ has a set $A\subseteq V(G)$ with $\chi(G[A])>\psi(\omega(G[A]))$ such that either $G[A]$ is $H$-free, or $G$ contains an induced copy of $H$ whose vertex set is disjoint from $A$ and has no edges to $A$. If $H_1$ and $H_2$ are forests such that the classes of $H_1$-free and $H_2$-free graphs are polynomially $\chi$-bounded and one of them is self-isolating, then the class of graphs with no induced copy of the disjoint union of $H_1$ and $H_2$ is polynomially $\chi$-bounded, which motivates the notion. A graph is self-isolating if all its components are; the only connected graphs known to be self-isolating are complete graphs and complete bipartite graphs (proved in the paper; the case of stars was proved earlier) and paths of arbitrary length. The authors know very few graphs with the property and none without it. If the polynomials $\phi,\psi$ in the definition are replaced by general functions, it is easy to show (by induction on $\omega(G)$) that all graphs have the property.
notes: Posed explicitly as a question in Section 2; no formal label.
paper_title: Polynomial bounds for chromatic number VII. Disjoint holes
